claim: EHD2 protein is overexpressed in a large subset of breast cancers, especially the triple-negative (TNBC) and HER2+ subtypes.
source: Here, we show that overexpression of the EPS15-Homology Domain-containing 2 (EHD2) protein in a large subset of breast cancers (BCs), especially the triple-negative (TNBC) and HER2+ subtypes, correlates with shorter patient survival.
evidence: Supported by IHC analysis of 840 primary BC samples showing high cytoplasmic EHD2 in about half of TNBC and HER2+ samples (Figure 3C), and immunoblotting showing EHD2 expression in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines and 3 out of 11 HER2+ cell lines (Figure 2A).

claim: EHD2 overexpression in breast cancers correlates with shorter patient survival.
source: Here, we show that overexpression of the EPS15-Homology Domain-containing 2 (EHD2) protein in a large subset of breast cancers (BCs), especially the triple-negative (TNBC) and HER2+ subtypes, correlates with shorter patient survival.
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed high cytoplasmic EHD2 predicted shorter BC-specific survival (Figure 3B).

claim: The mRNAs for EHD2 and Caveolin-1/2 show co-overexpression across breast tumors.
source: The mRNAs for EHD2 and Caveolin-1/2, structural components of caveolae, show co-overexpression across breast tumors, predicting shorter survival in basal-like BC.
evidence: bc-GenExMiner analysis of 5277 BC samples demonstrated tight co-expression of EHD2 with CAV1 and CAV2 in TNBC samples (Figure 7A).

claim: Co-overexpression of EHD2, CAV1, and CAV2 predicts shorter survival in basal-like breast cancer.
source: The mRNAs for EHD2 and Caveolin-1/2, structural components of caveolae, show co-overexpression across breast tumors, predicting shorter survival in basal-like BC.
evidence: KM Plotter analysis showed combined EHD2-, CAV1-, and CAV2-high basal (PAM50-based) BC patients had significantly shorter distal metastasis-free survival (Figure 7B).

claim: EHD2 shRNA knockdown and CRISPR-Cas9 knockout with mouse Ehd2 rescue demonstrate a major positive role of EHD2 in promoting tumorigenesis and metastasis in TNBC cell line models.
source: EHD2 shRNA knockdown and CRISPR-Cas9 knockout with mouse Ehd2 rescue, in TNBC cell line models demonstrate a major positive role of EHD2 in promoting tumorigenesis and metastasis.
evidence: EHD2 knockdown markedly reduced tumorsphere growth (Figure 4C), impaired invasion (Figure 4D-E), and severely reduced xenograft tumor formation (Figure 4F). EHD2 knockout significantly impaired migration, invasion (Figure 5B-C), ECM degradation (Figure 5D), and tumor formation, with rescue by mouse Ehd2 (Figure 5H).

claim: EHD2 promotes tumorigenesis and metastasis through regulation of store-operated calcium entry (SOCE).
source: Mechanistically, we link these roles of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), with EHD2-dependent stabilization of plasma membrane caveolae ensuring high cell surface expression of the SOCE-linked calcium channel Orai1.
evidence: EHD2-KO cells demonstrated marked defects in both Tg-induced Ca2+ release and SOCE (Figure 8A-B). EHD2-KO reduced cell surface Orai1 levels (Figure 9C). STIM1 overexpression partially rescued SOCE and migration defects in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9E-F).

claim: EHD2-dependent stabilization of plasma membrane caveolae ensures high cell surface expression of the SOCE-linked calcium channel Orai1.
source: Mechanistically, we link these roles of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), with EHD2-dependent stabilization of plasma membrane caveolae ensuring high cell surface expression of the SOCE-linked calcium channel Orai1.
evidence: TIRF microscopy showed significant reduction of cell surface CAV1-GFP puncta (caveolae) in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 7E). Cell surface biotinylation demonstrated marked reduction in cell surface Orai1 in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9C).

claim: The EHD2-SOCE oncogenic axis represents a potential therapeutic target in EHD2- and CAV1/2-overexpressing breast cancer.
source: The novel EHD2-SOCE oncogenic axis represents a potential therapeutic target in EHD2- and CAV1/2-overexpressing BC.
evidence: SOCE inhibitors SKF96365 and CM4620 significantly impaired TNBC cell migration (Figure 10A). SKF96365 treatment significantly reduced TNBC xenograft tumor growth (Figure 10B).

claim: Nearly all cancer deaths are a result of metastasis.
source: With nearly all cancer deaths a result of metastasis, elucidating novel pro-metastatic cellular adaptations could provide new therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is a general statement about cancer biology presented as established knowledge.

claim: Triple-negative breast cancer has less than 30% 5-year survival rate in patients with metastatic disease.
source: Breast cancer (BC) remains a major cause of cancer-related deaths, with less than 30% 5-year survival rate in patients with metastatic disease (https://www.acs.org/).
evidence: Cited from American Cancer Society website.

claim: Triple-negative breast cancer lacks targeted therapies.
source: Triple-negative BC (TNBC) presents a particularly difficult diagnosis with lack of targeted therapies.
evidence: This is presented as established clinical knowledge about TNBC.

claim: EHD proteins (EHD1-4) are evolutionarily conserved lipid membrane-activated ATPases.
source: EPS15-homology (EH) domain-containing (EHD) proteins (EHD1-4) are evolutionarily conserved lipid membrane-activated ATPases that regulate inward or outward vesicular traffic between the plasma membrane and intracellular organelles by controlling tubulation and scission of trafficking vesicles (Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011.

claim: EHD proteins regulate vesicular traffic between the plasma membrane and intracellular organelles by controlling tubulation and scission of trafficking vesicles.
source: EPS15-homology (EH) domain-containing (EHD) proteins (EHD1-4) are evolutionarily conserved lipid membrane-activated ATPases that regulate inward or outward vesicular traffic between the plasma membrane and intracellular organelles by controlling tubulation and scission of trafficking vesicles (Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Naslavsky and Caplan, 2011.

claim: EHD2 primarily localizes to plasma membrane caveolae to maintain their stable membrane pool.
source: Unlike other family members, which predominantly localize to endosomal and other intracellular compartments, EHD2 is known to primarily localizes to plasma membrane caveolae to maintain their stable membrane pool (Morén et al., 2012; Stoeber et al., 2012), suggesting a likely role in caveolae-associated cellular functions.
evidence: Supported by citations to Morén et al., 2012 and Stoeber et al., 2012.

claim: Caveolae-dependent fatty acid uptake in adipocytes is impaired in Ehd2 knockout mice.
source: Indeed, caveolae-dependent fatty acid uptake in adipocytes and eNOS-NO induced small blood vessel relaxation are impaired in Ehd2 knockout mice (Matthaeus et al., 2020; Matthaeus et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matthaeus et al., 2020 and Matthaeus et al., 2019.

claim: eNOS-NO induced small blood vessel relaxation is impaired in Ehd2 knockout mice.
source: Indeed, caveolae-dependent fatty acid uptake in adipocytes and eNOS-NO induced small blood vessel relaxation are impaired in Ehd2 knockout mice (Matthaeus et al., 2020; Matthaeus et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Matthaeus et al., 2020 and Matthaeus et al., 2019.

claim: EHD2-dependent stabilization of caveolae promotes cell surface expression of ATP-sensitive K+ channels and protects cardiomyocytes against ischemic injury.
source: EHD2-dependent stabilization of caveolae was also found to promote the cell surface expression of ATP-sensitive K+ channels and protect cardiomyocytes against ischemic injury (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Caveolae are key to buffering the plasma membrane stress.
source: Caveolae are key to buffering the plasma membrane stress (Sinha et al., 2011) and EHD2 has been shown to positively regulate mechano-transduction through re-localization to the nucleus and regulation of gene transcription (Torrino et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sinha et al., 2011.

claim: EHD2 positively regulates mechano-transduction through re-localization to the nucleus and regulation of gene transcription.
source: Caveolae are key to buffering the plasma membrane stress (Sinha et al., 2011) and EHD2 has been shown to positively regulate mechano-transduction through re-localization to the nucleus and regulation of gene transcription (Torrino et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torrino et al., 2018.

claim: Reduced EHD2 expression was reported in esophageal, colorectal, breast, and hepatocellular cancers.
source: Reduced EHD2 expression was reported in esophageal, colorectal, breast, and hepatocellular cancers (Li et al., 2013; Guan et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016), with in vitro knockdown or overexpression studies supporting a tumor suppressive role for EHD2.
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2013; Guan et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2016.

claim: EHD2 overexpression was found as a component of a mesenchymal signature in malignant gliomas with shorter survival.
source: On the contrary, EHD2 overexpression was found as a component of a mesenchymal signature in malignant gliomas with shorter survival, and knockdown analyses showed the EHD2 requirement for cell proliferation, migration, and invasion (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: EHD2 knockdown in malignant gliomas showed EHD2 requirement for cell proliferation, migration, and invasion.
source: On the contrary, EHD2 overexpression was found as a component of a mesenchymal signature in malignant gliomas with shorter survival, and knockdown analyses showed the EHD2 requirement for cell proliferation, migration, and invasion (Zhang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2021.

claim: Higher EHD2 mRNA expression in papillary thyroid carcinomas was associated with extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastasis, higher risk of recurrence, and presence of BRAF-V600E mutation.
source: Higher EHD2 mRNA expression in papillary thyroid carcinomas was associated with extrathyroidal extension, lymph node metastasis, higher risk of recurrence, and presence of BRAF-V600E mutation (Kim et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2017.

claim: Studies of clear cell renal cell carcinoma supported a positive role of EHD2 in tumorigenesis.
source: Studies of clear cell renal cell carcinoma also supported a positive role of EHD2 in tumorigenesis (Liu et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2019.

claim: Loss of EHD2 expression in TNBC cell lines enhanced their proliferation, migration, and invasion.
source: A recent study provided a more mixed picture, with loss of EHD2 expression in TNBC cell lines enhancing their proliferation, migration, and invasion but low levels of EHD2 mRNA in TNBC patient tumors predicting better prognosis (Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2020.

claim: Low levels of EHD2 mRNA in TNBC patient tumors predicted better prognosis.
source: A recent study provided a more mixed picture, with loss of EHD2 expression in TNBC cell lines enhancing their proliferation, migration, and invasion but low levels of EHD2 mRNA in TNBC patient tumors predicting better prognosis (Shen et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Shen et al., 2020.

claim: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) is a pathway known to promote tumorigenesis and metastasis in breast and other cancers.
source: Our studies suggest a novel pro-oncogenic mechanism of EHD2, namely its requirement for efficient store-operated calcium entry (SOCE), a pathway known to promote tumorigenesis and metastasis in breast and other cancers (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mo and Yang, 2018 and Yang et al., 2009.

claim: EHD2 is expressed in basal cells of the mouse mammary gland.
source: EHD2 is expressed in basal cells of the mouse mammary gland and in a subset of basal-like breast cancer cell lines
evidence: Immunofluorescence showed moderate/high EHD2 staining in mammary basal/myo-epithelium (smooth muscle actin+), but little in luminal epithelium (cytokeratin 8+; Figure 1C). IHC confirmed basal/myoepithelial cell selective localization (Figure 1D).

claim: High EHD2 expression is seen in mammary adipocytes.
source: High EHD2 expression was seen in mammary adipocytes, consistent with high EHD2 expression in adipose tissues (Morén et al., 2019).
evidence: Immunofluorescence staining showed high EHD2 expression in mammary adipocytes (Figure 1B), consistent with citation to Morén et al., 2019.

claim: Within the mammary epithelium, basal epithelial cells selectively express higher EHD2 levels.
source: Thus, while mammary adipocytes express the highest levels of EHD2, within the epithelium the basal epithelial cells selectively express higher EHD2 levels.
evidence: Immunoblotting of basal and luminal mouse mammary epithelial cell-derived organoids confirmed basal cell expression of EHD2 (Figure 1E).

claim: EHD2 is expressed in immortal basal-like mammary epithelial cell lines 76Ntert and MCF10A.
source: By immunoblotting, we found EHD2 expression in immortal basal-like mammary epithelial cell lines 76Ntert (hTert-immortalized primary mammary epithelial cell line; Zhao et al., 2010) and MCF10A, in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines, and at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2 + cell lines, but in none of the 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed EHD2 expression in these cell lines (Figure 2A).

claim: EHD2 is expressed in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines.
source: By immunoblotting, we found EHD2 expression in immortal basal-like mammary epithelial cell lines 76Ntert (hTert-immortalized primary mammary epithelial cell line; Zhao et al., 2010) and MCF10A, in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines, and at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2 + cell lines, but in none of the 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed EHD2 expression in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines (Figure 2A).

claim: EHD2 is expressed at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2+ cell lines.
source: By immunoblotting, we found EHD2 expression in immortal basal-like mammary epithelial cell lines 76Ntert (hTert-immortalized primary mammary epithelial cell line; Zhao et al., 2010) and MCF10A, in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines, and at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2 + cell lines, but in none of the 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed EHD2 expression at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2+ cell lines (Figure 2A).

claim: EHD2 is not expressed in any of the 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines tested.
source: By immunoblotting, we found EHD2 expression in immortal basal-like mammary epithelial cell lines 76Ntert (hTert-immortalized primary mammary epithelial cell line; Zhao et al., 2010) and MCF10A, in 2 out of 3 TNBC cell lines, and at lower levels in 3 out of 11 HER2 + cell lines, but in none of the 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines (Figure 2A).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed no EHD2 expression in 9 luminal A/B BC cell lines (Figure 2A).

claim: EHD2 localizes exclusively to the plasma membrane and cytoplasm in breast cancer cell lines.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of selected cell lines confirmed the expression pattern seen in immunoblotting and showed exclusive localization of EHD2 to the plasma membrane and cytoplasm (Figure 2B).
evidence: Immunofluorescence microscopy showed predominant cytoplasmic and membrane localization of EHD2 (Figure 2B).

claim: The pattern of EHD2 protein expression in breast cancer cell lines correlates with EHD2 mRNA expression data in the CCLE database.
source: The pattern of EHD2 protein expression we observed correlated with the EHD2 mRNA expression data in the CCLE database (Dai et al., 2017; Figure 2C).
evidence: Comparison of immunoblotting results with CCLE mRNA data showed correlation (Figure 2C), with citation to Dai et al., 2017.

claim: Higher EHD2 mRNA expression is a feature of TNBC cell lines, especially the mesenchymal-type.
source: Furthermore, by relating the CCLE data to the reported BC cell line subtype analysis (Lehmann et al., 2011), we found higher EHD2 mRNA expression to be a feature of TNBC cell lines, especially the mesenchymal-type (Figure 2D), similar to our western blot results (Figure 2A) where both EHD2-expressing TNBC cell lines were of the mesenchymal-type Figure 2D.
evidence: Analysis of CCLE data related to BC cell line subtypes showed higher EHD2 mRNA in TNBC, especially mesenchymal-type (Figure 2D), with citation to Lehmann et al., 2011.

claim: High EHD2 expression is a feature of normal basal mammary epithelial cells and a subset of the basal-like/triple-negative breast cancer.
source: Thus, high EHD2 expression is a feature of normal basal mammary epithelial cells and a subset of the basal-like/triple-negative BC.
evidence: Based on expression patterns in mouse mammary gland (Figure 1) and BC cell lines (Figure 2).

claim: 759 breast cancer cases showed a valid positive/negative cytoplasmic EHD2 signal in the tissue microarray analysis.
source: 759 and 756 cases respectively showed a valid positive/negative cytoplasmic or nuclear signal (Supplementary file 1-Table 1A).
evidence: IHC staining of TMA with 840 primary BC samples yielded 759 valid cases for cytoplasmic scoring.

claim: 756 breast cancer cases showed a valid positive/negative nuclear EHD2 signal in the tissue microarray analysis.
source: 759 and 756 cases respectively showed a valid positive/negative cytoplasmic or nuclear signal (Supplementary file 1-Table 1A).
evidence: IHC staining of TMA with 840 primary BC samples yielded 756 valid cases for nuclear scoring.

claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 signal is positively associated with higher tumor grade, higher mitosis, and lower cytokeratin-5 expression.
source: High cytoplasmic and low nuclear EHD2 signals showed a positive association with higher tumor grade, higher mitosis, and lower cyokeratin-5 expression while high nuclear and low cytoplasmic EHD2 signals showed a reverse correlation and was associated with ER/PR/AR-positive and non-TNBC status (Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of IHC data showed these associations (Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).

claim: High nuclear and low cytoplasmic EHD2 signals are associated with ER/PR/AR-positive and non-TNBC status.
source: High cytoplasmic and low nuclear EHD2 signals showed a positive association with higher tumor grade, higher mitosis, and lower cyokeratin-5 expression while high nuclear and low cytoplasmic EHD2 signals showed a reverse correlation and was associated with ER/PR/AR-positive and non-TNBC status (Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).
evidence: Statistical analysis of IHC data showed these associations (Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).

claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 predicted shorter breast cancer-specific survival.
source: High cytoplasmic EHD2 predicted shorter BC-specific survival, while high nuclear EHD2 showed an opposite correlation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed high cytoplasmic EHD2 correlated with shorter survival (Figure 3B).

claim: High nuclear EHD2 predicted longer breast cancer-specific survival.
source: High cytoplasmic EHD2 predicted shorter BC-specific survival, while high nuclear EHD2 showed an opposite correlation (Figure 3B).
evidence: Kaplan-Meier survival analysis showed high nuclear EHD2 correlated with longer survival (Figure 3B).

claim: High cytoplasmic and nuclear-negative EHD2 was seen in about half of TNBC and HER2+ samples.
source: Across BC subtypes, the high cytoplasmic and nuclear-negative EHD2, which also predicted shorter BC-specific survival (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), was seen in about half of TNBC and HER2 + samples, and a third of ER + samples (Figure 3C, Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).
evidence: Analysis of IHC data across BC subtypes showed this distribution (Figure 3C).

claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 expression is strongly skewed in basal-like TNBC.
source: Analysis of a subset of our patient cohort with data for further subtyping showed a strong skewing of high cytoplasmic EHD2 expression in basal-like TNBC and to some extent the HER2-enriched and luminal B subtypes, while high nuclear EHD2 expression was a feature of luminal A subtype (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Subtype analysis of patient cohort showed high cytoplasmic EHD2 in basal-like TNBC (Figure 3D-E).

claim: High nuclear EHD2 expression is a feature of luminal A breast cancer subtype.
source: Analysis of a subset of our patient cohort with data for further subtyping showed a strong skewing of high cytoplasmic EHD2 expression in basal-like TNBC and to some extent the HER2-enriched and luminal B subtypes, while high nuclear EHD2 expression was a feature of luminal A subtype (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: Subtype analysis of patient cohort showed high nuclear EHD2 in luminal A subtype (Figure 3D-E).

claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 expression is a marker of more aggressive breast cancer.
source: Thus, our results indicate that high cytoplasmic EHD2 expression, a localization similar to that observed in normal mouse mammary epithelium and human BC cell lines, is a marker of more aggressive BC, contrary to published reports that did not assess the cytoplasmic/nuclear distribution of EHD2 and suggested its potential tumor suppressor role (Yang et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on associations with higher tumor grade, higher mitosis, and shorter survival (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1-Table 1B).

claim: EHD2 knockdown did not affect proliferation in two-dimensional culture on plastic.
source: While EHD2 knockdown (KD) did not affect proliferation in two-dimensional culture on plastic (Figure 4B), it markedly reduced the tumorsphere growth under low attachment (Figure 4C), impaired invasion across Matrigel in trans-well assays (Figure 4D) and markedly reduced the invasive fronts in a Matrigel organoid invasion assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: Cell Titer-Glo proliferation assay showed no significant difference between control and EHD2 shRNA cells (Figure 4B).

claim: EHD2 knockdown markedly reduced tumorsphere growth under low attachment conditions.
source: While EHD2 knockdown (KD) did not affect proliferation in two-dimensional culture on plastic (Figure 4B), it markedly reduced the tumorsphere growth under low attachment (Figure 4C), impaired invasion across Matrigel in trans-well assays (Figure 4D) and markedly reduced the invasive fronts in a Matrigel organoid invasion assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: Tumorsphere formation assay showed significant reduction with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4C).

claim: EHD2 knockdown impaired invasion across Matrigel in trans-well assays.
source: While EHD2 knockdown (KD) did not affect proliferation in two-dimensional culture on plastic (Figure 4B), it markedly reduced the tumorsphere growth under low attachment (Figure 4C), impaired invasion across Matrigel in trans-well assays (Figure 4D) and markedly reduced the invasive fronts in a Matrigel organoid invasion assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: Transwell invasion assay showed significant reduction with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4D).

claim: EHD2 knockdown markedly reduced invasive fronts in a Matrigel organoid invasion assay.
source: While EHD2 knockdown (KD) did not affect proliferation in two-dimensional culture on plastic (Figure 4B), it markedly reduced the tumorsphere growth under low attachment (Figure 4C), impaired invasion across Matrigel in trans-well assays (Figure 4D) and markedly reduced the invasive fronts in a Matrigel organoid invasion assay (Figure 4E).
evidence: Three-dimensional invasion assay showed significant reduction in spheroids with invasive fronts with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4E).

claim: Orthotopically implanted control Hs578T cells produced xenograft tumors while EHD2 knockdown cells showed severe reduction in tumor formation.
source: Orthotopically implanted control Hs578T cells produced xenograft tumors over time while EHD2 KD cells showed a severe reduction in tumor formation (Figure 4F).
evidence: Xenograft tumorigenesis assay showed significant reduction in tumor volume with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4F).

claim: EHD2 knockdown in xenograft tumors showed marked reduction in proliferation (Ki67+).
source: Immunostaining confirmed the EHD2 KD (Figure 4G) and showed marked reduction in proliferation (Ki67+) with sparse tumor cells in H&E sections (Figure 4H).
evidence: IHC staining of tumor sections showed marked reduction in Ki67+ cells with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4H).

claim: EHD2 knockdown in MDA-MB-231 cells reduced xenograft growth and frequency of lung tumor metastasis.
source: EHD2 KD in MDA-MB-231 cells also reduced the xenograft growth and frequency of lung tumor metastasis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Xenograft and metastasis analysis showed reduced primary tumor growth and lung metastases with EHD2 knockdown (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).

claim: CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout in TNBC cell lines was not associated with significant changes in EHD1/4 expression.
source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
evidence: Immunoblot analysis showed no significant changes in EHD1/4 expression in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).

claim: EHD2 knockout significantly impaired migration and invasion of TNBC cells.
source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
evidence: Transwell migration and invasion assays showed significant impairment with EHD2 knockout (Figure 5B-C).

claim: EHD2 knockout significantly impaired extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability of TNBC cells.
source: Further, CRISPR-Cas9-mediated EHD2 knockout (KO) in TNBC cell lines (Figure 5A), which unlike our observations in Ehd2-KO mouse tissues was not associated with any significant changes in EHD1/4 expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), significantly impaired their migration, invasion (Figure 5B–C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–B) and extracellular matrix (ECM) degradation ability (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2C), another pro-metastatic trait (Cheung and Ewald, 2014).
evidence: ECM degradation assay showed significant reduction with EHD2 knockout (Figure 5D), with citation to Cheung and Ewald, 2014 for ECM degradation as a pro-metastatic trait.

claim: Introduction of mouse Ehd2 in MDA-MB-231 EHD2-KO cells significantly rescued the cell migration defect.
source: Introduction of mouse Ehd2 in MDA-MB-231 EHD2-KO cells, at levels lower than in control cells, significantly rescued the cell migration defect (Figure 5E), demonstrating specificity.
evidence: Mouse Ehd2 rescue experiment showed significant rescue of migration defect (Figure 5E).

claim: CRISPR activation of endogenous EHD2 in EHD2-nonexpressing MDA-MB-468 TNBC cells increased cell migration compared to control cells.
source: Reciprocally, CRISPR activation of endogenous EHD2 in EHD2-nonexpressing MDA-MB-468 TNBC cells (Figure 5F) increased cell migration compared to control cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: CRISPRa induction of EHD2 in MDA-MB-468 cells increased migration (Figure 5F-G).

claim: EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells exhibited a marked and significant defect in orthotopic tumor formation, with significant rescue upon mouse Ehd2 expression.
source: When orthotopically implanted in nude mice, EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells exhibited a marked and significant defect in tumor formation, with a significant rescue upon mouse Ehd2 expression (Figure 5H).
evidence: Xenograft tumorigenesis assay showed marked defect in EHD2-KO cells with rescue by mouse Ehd2 (Figure 5H).

claim: Intravenously injected control MDA-MB-231 cells showed time-dependent lung metastatic growth while EHD2-KO cells showed no growth or reduction in signals.
source: Luminescence bioimaging showed time-dependent lung metastatic growth of control cells but no growth (or a reduction in signals) with EHD2-KO cells (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: Bioluminescence imaging showed lung metastatic growth in control but not EHD2-KO cells (Figure 6A-C).

claim: EHD2-KO MDA-MB-231 cells showed nearly complete absence of metastatic nodules in lungs at necropsy.
source: These findings were confirmed by assessment of lung metastatic nodules at necropsy (Figure 6D).
evidence: Quantification of tumor nodules in lungs showed nearly complete absence in EHD2-KO group (Figure 6D).

claim: EHD2 and CAV1 mRNAs show tight co-expression in TNBC samples.
source: The bc-GenExMiner analysis of 5277 BC samples Jézéquel et al., 2013 demonstrated tight co-expression of EHD2 with the structural components of caveolae, CAV1 and CAV2 in TNBC samples (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: bc-GenExMiner analysis showed Pearson's correlation of R=0.7 for EHD2/CAV1 in TNBC (Figure 7A), with citation to Jézéquel et al., 2013.

claim: EHD2 and CAV2 mRNAs show tight co-expression in TNBC samples.
source: The bc-GenExMiner analysis of 5277 BC samples Jézéquel et al., 2013 demonstrated tight co-expression of EHD2 with the structural components of caveolae, CAV1 and CAV2 in TNBC samples (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: bc-GenExMiner analysis showed Pearson's correlation of R=0.51 for EHD2/CAV2 in TNBC (Figure 7A), with citation to Jézéquel et al., 2013.

claim: Combined EHD2-, CAV1-, and CAV2-high basal BC patients showed significantly shorter distal metastasis-free survival.
source: By KM Plotter analysis, combined EHD2-, CAV1-, and CAV2-high basal (PAM50-based) but not all BC patients showed significantly shorter distal metastasis-free survival (Figure 7B, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: KM Plotter analysis showed shorter relapse-free survival in basal-like BC with high EHD2, CAV1, and CAV2 (Figure 7B).

claim: EHD2 and CAV1 show concordant expression in mammary epithelial and breast cancer cell lines.
source: Immunoblotting demonstrated concordant EHD2 and CAV1 expression in mammary epithelial and BC cell lines (Figure 7C).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed coordinate EHD2 and CAV1 expression across cell lines (Figure 7C).

claim: EHD2 and CAV1 show a high degree of colocalization in TNBC cell lines.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis using structured illumination microscopy (SIM) demonstrated a high degree of colocalization between EHD2 and CAV1 in TNBC cell lines (Figure 7D).
evidence: SIM images showed colocalization of EHD2 and CAV1 with Pearson's Coefficient of Colocalization around 0.6-0.7 (Figure 7D).

claim: EHD2-KO cells show a significant reduction of cell surface associated CAV1-GFP puncta (caveolae).
source: Total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy analysis showed a significant reduction of cell surface associated CAV1-GFP puncta, representing cell surface caveolae, in EHD2-KO compared to control Hs578T cells (Figure 7E), consistent with the reported electron microcopy-based high cell surface caveolae density on Hs578T compared to a lower density on the EHD2-non-expressing MDA-MB-436 cells (Torrino et al., 2018).
evidence: TIRF microscopy showed significant reduction in CAV1 puncta per cell in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 7E), consistent with citation to Torrino et al., 2018.

claim: CAV1 knockout led to significant impairment of cell migration in TNBC cells.
source: CRISPR KO of CAV1 (Figure 7F) led to a significant impairment of cell migration like that with EHD2-KO (Figure 7G).
evidence: Transwell migration assay showed significant reduction with CAV1-KO (Figure 7G).

claim: EHD2-dependent maintenance of cell surface caveolae is linked to its promotion of tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits.
source: These results support the conclusion that EHD2-dependent maintenance of cell surface caveolae is linked to its promotion of tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits, although the potential role(s) of EHD2 and caveolae in other subcellular locations cannot be excluded at present.
evidence: Based on co-expression, colocalization, and functional effects of EHD2 and CAV1 knockout (Figure 7).

claim: Store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) operates at caveolae.
source: We investigated the linkage of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) (Chung et al., 2017), a pathway that operates at caveolae (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017) and is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Pani and Singh, 2009 and Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017.

claim: SOCE is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers.
source: We investigated the linkage of EHD2 to store-operated calcium entry (SOCE) (Chung et al., 2017), a pathway that operates at caveolae (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017) and is a well-established pro-metastatic signaling pathway in TNBC and other cancers (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mo and Yang, 2018 and Yang et al., 2009.

claim: SOCE is mediated by translocation of ER Ca2+ sensor STIM1 to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion.
source: The SOCE is mediated by translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion which permits its binding to and activation of the Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel to promote Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: STIM1 binding to and activation of Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel promotes Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER.
source: The SOCE is mediated by translocation of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) Ca2+ sensor stromal-interaction molecule 1 (STIM1) to ER-plasma membrane contact sites upon ER Ca2+ depletion which permits its binding to and activation of the Orai1 membrane Ca2+ channel to promote Ca2+ entry for Ca2+-dependent signaling and refilling of the ER (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Control TNBC cells exhibited a robust rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ upon thapsigargin treatment in Ca2+-free medium.
source: Expectedly, control Hs578T or BT549 TNBC cells exhibited a robust rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ that declined over time (Figure 8A–B), reflecting the release of ER Ca2+ (Ong et al., 2007).
evidence: Fluo4-AM loaded cells showed robust Ca2+ rise upon thapsigargin treatment (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Ong et al., 2007.

claim: Addition of Ca2+ in the medium after thapsigargin treatment induced a rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+, indicating SOCE.
source: Subsequent addition of Ca2+ in the medium induced a rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+, indicating the SOCE (Figure 8A–B; Ong et al., 2007).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed rapid increase in cytoplasmic Ca2+ upon Ca2+ addition (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Ong et al., 2007.

claim: Pre-treatment with SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 markedly reduced the initial Ca2+ flux and nearly abrogated the SOCE.
source: Pre-treatment with the SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 (Yang et al., 2009) markedly reduced the initial Ca2+ flux and nearly abrogated the SOCE (Figure 8C).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay with SKF96365 pre-treatment showed marked reduction in both phases (Figure 8C), with citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: EHD2-KO cells demonstrated a marked defect in both the initial Tg-induced rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ and the subsequent SOCE.
source: EHD2-KO cells demonstrated a marked defect in both the initial Tg-induced rise in cytoplasmic Ca2+ and the subsequent SOCE (Figure 8A–B), consistent with the established role of SOCE in intracellular Ca2+ store filling (the source of the initial Ca2+ release upon Tg treatment) besides Ca2+-dependent signaling (Chung et al., 2017).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assays showed marked defects in both phases in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8A-B), with citation to Chung et al., 2017.

claim: Defective SOCE was observed in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells using cyclopiazonic acid (CPA).
source: Defective SOCE was also seen in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells using another SERCA inhibitor cyclopiazonic acid (CPA) (Demaurex et al., 1992; Figure 8D).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay with CPA showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8D), with citation to Demaurex et al., 1992.

claim: EHD2-KO Hs578T cells expressing GCaMP6s exhibited defective Tg-induced SOCE.
source: In a genetic approach, we showed that EHD2-KO Hs578T cells stably expressing a GFP-based reporter of cytoplasmic Ca2+, GCaMP6s, (Chen et al., 2013), exhibited defective Tg-induced SOCE (Figure 8E, Figure 8—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay using GCaMP6s reporter showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8E), with citation to Chen et al., 2013.

claim: EHD2-KO Hs578T cells expressing GCaMP6s-CAAX showed defective SOCE.
source: Further, stable expression of GCaMP6s-CAAX, a plasma membrane-targeted fluorescent reporter of Ca2+ levels (Tsai et al., 2014), which only detects the SOCE phase upon Tg treatment directly established the defective SOCE in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 8F, Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay using GCaMP6s-CAAX reporter showed defective SOCE in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 8F), with citation to Tsai et al., 2014.

claim: CRISPRa-induced endogenous EHD2 expression in EHD2-negative MDA-MB-468 cells led to a marked increase in Tg-induced SOCE.
source: In a reciprocal experiment, CRISPRa- induced endogenous EHD2 expression in EHD2-negative MDA-MB-468 cells led to a marked increase in Tg-induced SOCE (Figure 8G).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed marked increase in SOCE with CRISPRa-induced EHD2 expression (Figure 8G).

claim: A marked defect in SOCE was observed in CAV1-KO TNBC cell lines.
source: Consistent with the role of caveolae, a marked defect in SOCE was observed in CAV1-KO TNBC cell lines (Figure 8H–I).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assays showed marked defects in SOCE in CAV1-KO cells (Figure 8H-I).

claim: Thapsigargin treatment failed to increase STIM1 puncta at the cell surface in EHD2-KO cells.
source: Tg treatment failed to increase the STIM1 puncta in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9A).
evidence: TIRF microscopy showed no increase in STIM1 puncta with thapsigargin treatment in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9A).

claim: The defect in STIM1 puncta formation in EHD2-KO cells was not a result of reduced levels of total STIM1 and Orai1 proteins.
source: This defect was not a result of reduced levels of total STIM1 and Orai1 proteins (Figure 9B).
evidence: Immunoblotting showed comparable total STIM1 and Orai1 levels in control vs EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9B).

claim: Orai1 localizes in caveolae.
source: Given the known localization of Orai1 in caveolae (Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017; Sathish et al., 2012), we assessed the impact of EHD2-KO on Orai1 cell surface levels.
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017 and Sathish et al., 2012.

claim: EHD2-KO cells showed a marked reduction in cell surface Orai1 levels.
source: In contrast, streptavidin blotting revealed a marked reduction in biotinylated (cell surface) Orai1 signals in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9C, upper panels).
evidence: Cell surface biotinylation followed by Orai1 immunoprecipitation showed marked reduction in surface Orai1 in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 9C).

claim: Overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells partially rescued the SOCE defect.
source: Further linking the SOCE to EHD2-dependent pro-metastatic traits, overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 9D) partially rescued the SOCE defect (Figure 9E) and the defective cell migration (Figure 9F).
evidence: Ca2+ flux assay showed partial rescue of SOCE with STIM1 overexpression (Figure 9E).

claim: Overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells partially rescued the defective cell migration.
source: Further linking the SOCE to EHD2-dependent pro-metastatic traits, overexpression of CFP-STIM1 in EHD2-KO Hs578T cells (Figure 9D) partially rescued the SOCE defect (Figure 9E) and the defective cell migration (Figure 9F).
evidence: Transwell migration assay showed partial rescue with STIM1 overexpression (Figure 9F).

claim: SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 significantly impaired wildtype TNBC cell migration.
source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
evidence: Transwell migration assay with SKF96365 showed significant reduction in wildtype TNBC cell migration (Figure 10A), with citation to Bruen et al., 2022 for CM4620.

claim: SOCE inhibitor CM4620 significantly impaired wildtype TNBC cell migration.
source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
evidence: Transwell migration assay with CM4620 showed significant reduction in wildtype TNBC cell migration (Figure 10A), with citation to Bruen et al., 2022.

claim: CM4620 (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions.
source: In a complementary approach, the tool SOCE inhibitor SKF96365 and a recently identified inhibitor CM4620, which (as Auxora, CalciMedica) has progressed to phase 3 clinical trials in acute inflammatory disease conditions (Bruen et al., 2022), significantly impaired the wildtype TNBC cell migration, and further reduced the migration of EHD2-KO cells, albeit the latter was not statistically significant (Figure 10A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bruen et al., 2022.

claim: A major proportion of the SOCE in TNBC cell lines is dependent on EHD2 and is inhibitable with available SOCE inhibitors.
source: Thus, a major proportion of the SOCE in TNBC cell lines is dependent on EHD2 and is inhibitable with available SOCE inhibitors.
evidence: Based on marked defects in SOCE with EHD2-KO (Figure 8) and significant inhibition with SKF96365 and CM4620 (Figure 10A).

claim: SKF96365 treatment significantly reduced control TNBC xenograft tumor growth.
source: Accordingly, we show that SKF96365 treatment significantly reduced the control TNBC xenograft tumor growth (Figure 10B); we were unable to test the SOCE inhibitor against EHD2-KO TNBC xenografts as these did not grow sufficiently to test the inhibitor impact.
evidence: Xenograft tumor growth assay showed significant reduction with SKF96365 treatment (Figure 10B).

claim: EHD2, by stabilizing caveolae, facilitates SOCE to promote downstream pro-oncogenic traits in TNBC cells.
source: Collectively, these findings support our conclusion that EHD2, by stabilizing caveolae, facilitates the SOCE to promote downstream pro-oncogenic traits in TNBC cells.
evidence: Based on collective findings showing EHD2 stabilizes caveolae (Figure 7E), regulates SOCE (Figure 8-9), and promotes oncogenic traits (Figure 4-6).

claim: High cytoplasmic EHD2 expression was found in a substantial proportion of breast tumors.
source: Our IHC analyses demonstrated high cytoplasmic EHD2 expression in a substantial proportion of breast tumors, associated with shorter BC-specific patient survival (Figure 3B) and higher tumor grade (Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
evidence: IHC analysis of 840 BC samples showed high cytoplasmic EHD2 in substantial proportion (Figure 3).

claim: A higher proportion of TNBC, luminal B and HER2+ patients exhibited high cytoplasmic EHD2.
source: A higher proportion of TNBC, luminal B and HER2 + patients exhibited high cytoplasmic EHD2 (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
evidence: Analysis of IHC data across BC subtypes showed this distribution (Figure 3D, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).

claim: Previous studies reported reduction in EHD2 expression correlates with tumor progression in breast cancer.
source: Our results differ from reports that reduction in EHD2 expression correlates with tumor progression in BC (Yang et al., 2015; Shi et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yang et al., 2015 and Shi et al., 2015.

claim: High EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes could result in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting.
source: Several factors could account for the discordance, including the lack of validation of antibodies in prior studies, the high EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes (Figure 1B), resulting in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting (Yang et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015), and the possibility that EHD2 signals in prior studies represented nuclear EHD2, which we find is associated with positive prognostic factors (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from high adipocyte EHD2 expression (Figure 1B) and discordance with prior western blot studies.

claim: EHD2 signals in prior studies may have represented nuclear EHD2, which is associated with positive prognostic factors.
source: Several factors could account for the discordance, including the lack of validation of antibodies in prior studies, the high EHD2 expression in normal mammary adipocytes (Figure 1B), resulting in apparent reduction in EHD2 expression in tumor tissue using western blotting (Yang et al., 2015; Shen et al., 2020; Shi et al., 2015), and the possibility that EHD2 signals in prior studies represented nuclear EHD2, which we find is associated with positive prognostic factors (Figure 3B, Supplementary file 1-Table 1).
evidence: Inferred from finding that nuclear EHD2 is associated with positive prognosis (Figure 3B) and prior studies did not distinguish nuclear vs cytoplasmic EHD2.

claim: EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals.
source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claim: Nuclear EHD2 exit is dependent on its SUMOylation.
source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claim: Nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains.
source: Previous cell-line-based studies have shown that EHD2 shuttles between the nucleus and cytoplasm based on nuclear import and exit signals, the latter dependent on its SUMOylation, and that nuclear EHD2 repressed transcription from fused transactivation domains (Pekar et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pekar et al., 2012.

claim: Application of mechanical stress to cells led to EHD2 release from caveolae, its SUMOylation and nuclear translocation where it regulated transcription of several genes including caveolar components.
source: Another study found that application of mechanical stress to cells led to EHD2 release from caveolae, its SUMOylation and nuclear translocation where it regulated transcription of several genes including caveolar components, in a potential positive feedback mechanism (Torrino et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Torrino et al., 2018.

claim: Nuclear translocation of EHD2 may sequester EHD2 to inhibit its plasma membrane-associated pro-oncogenic role in SOCE.
source: In view of the opposite prognostic significance of nuclear vs. non-nuclear EHD2 in our analyses of BC patient samples, it could be speculated that nuclear translocation may sequester EHD2 to inhibit its plasma membrane-associated pro-oncogenic role in SOCE, but rigorous studies will be needed to test this suggestion.
evidence: Speculated based on opposite prognostic significance of nuclear vs cytoplasmic EHD2 (Figure 3B).

claim: EHD2 is required for tumorigenesis under stringent conditions (tumorspheres).
source: We show that in vitro tumor cell growth under stringent conditions (tumorspheres; Figure 4C) and pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D–E–5B–D) are EHD2-dependent.
evidence: Tumorsphere assay showed EHD2 knockdown markedly reduced tumorsphere growth (Figure 4C).

claim: Pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation are EHD2-dependent.
source: We show that in vitro tumor cell growth under stringent conditions (tumorspheres; Figure 4C) and pro-metastatic traits of cell migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D–E–5B–D) are EHD2-dependent.
evidence: Multiple assays showed EHD2 knockdown or knockout impaired migration, invasion, and ECM degradation (Figures 4D-E, 5B-D).

claim: Extranuclear EHD2 overexpression in breast cancer cells represents a key pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic adaptation.
source: Although further studies are needed to fully dissect the steps at which EHD2 is critical in the metastatic process, collectively, our analyses conclusively demonstrate that extranuclear EHD2 overexpression in BC cells represents a key pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic adaptation.
evidence: Based on collective in vitro and in vivo data showing EHD2 promotes tumorigenesis and metastasis (Figures 4-6).

claim: EHD2 stabilizes caveolae.
source: Mechanistically, we link the EHD2 overexpression in BC cells to regulation of caveolae, whose stability is known to be controlled by EHD2 (Morén et al., 2012; Stoeber et al., 2012; Morén et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to Morén et al., 2012; Stoeber et al., 2012; Morén et al., 2019, and TIRF data showing reduced caveolae in EHD2-KO cells (Figure 7E).

claim: CAV1 has pro-tumorigenic roles in TNBC.
source: This includes the strong EHD2 co-localization with CAV1/2 (Figure 7D), reduction in cell surface caveolae density using TIRF microscopy upon EHD2-KO (Figure 7E), and inhibition of TNBC cell migration upon CAV1-KO (Figure 7G), consistent with the previously documented pro-tumorigenic roles of CAV1 in TNBC (Badana et al., 2016; Zou et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Badana et al., 2016 and Zou et al., 2017.

claim: CAV1 localizes in various intracellular locations besides the plasma membrane.
source: However, since our localization analyses show both EHD2 and CAV1 to also localize intracellularly besides at the plasma membrane (Figure 7D), and prior studies have identified pro-oncogenic roles for CAV1 localized in various intracellular locations (Simón et al., 2020), further studies will be needed to determine if the role of EHD2 we define here is exclusively related to regulation of the plasma membrane caveolae or might involve CAV1 in other compartments as well.
evidence: Supported by citation to Simón et al., 2020 and SIM images showing intracellular localization (Figure 7D).

claim: Caveolae serve as hubs for signaling.
source: Caveolae serve as hubs for signaling (Lamaze et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Lamaze et al., 2017.

claim: SOCE pathway regulates multiple tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits in TNBC.
source: Among these, the SOCE pathway stood out as it is known to regulate multiple tumorigenic and pro-metastatic traits in TNBC (Pani and Singh, 2009; Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017), as with EHD2 depletion.
evidence: Supported by citations to Pani and Singh, 2009 and Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017.

claim: EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins.
source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posey et al., 2011.

claim: Ferlins are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair.
source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Posey et al., 2011.

claim: EHD2 accumulates at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models.
source: Also, EHD2 interacts with Ca2+-binding proteins such as Ferlins (Posey et al., 2011) that are involved in Ca2+-dependent membrane repair and EHD2 was found to accumulate at sites of membrane repair in skeletal muscle models (Marg et al., 2012; Demonbreun et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Marg et al., 2012 and Demonbreun et al., 2016.

claim: EHD2 is a major positive regulator of SOCE in TNBC cell models.
source: Indeed, our extensive analyses demonstrate that EHD2 is a major positive regulator of SOCE in TNBC cell models.
evidence: Based on multiple Ca2+ flux assays showing marked defects in SOCE with EHD2-KO and increases with EHD2 overexpression (Figure 8).

claim: SOCE plays a role in intracellular Ca2+ store refilling.
source: Consistent with the established role of SOCE in the intracellular Ca2+ store refilling (Chung et al., 2017), which then serves as the source of the initial Ca2+ release upon appropriate stimuli (Tg or CPA in our studies), loss of EHD2 or CAV1 expression or treatment with SOCE inhibitors led to an impairment of the SOCE as well as the initial Ca2+ peak (Figure 8A–E; Figure 8H–I).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chung et al., 2017 and Ca2+ flux data (Figure 8).

claim: Orai1 is a major STIM1-interacting caveolae-resident SOCE channel.
source: Orai1 is a major STIM1-interacting caveolae-resident SOCE channel (Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017; Sathish et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bohórquez-Hernández et al., 2017 and Sathish et al., 2012.

claim: EHD2-dependent stabilization of cell surface caveolae ensures high cell surface levels of Orai1 to enable robust SOCE in TNBCs.
source: Thus, our findings support a model whereby EHD2-dependent stabilization of cell surface caveolae ensures high cell surface levels of Orai1 to enable robust SOCE in TNBCs, which in turn promotes pro-tumorigenic and pro-metastatic behaviors of tumor cells (Mo and Yang, 2018; Yang et al., 2009).
evidence: Based on findings that EHD2-KO reduces cell surface caveolae (Figure 7E), reduces cell surface Orai1 (Figure 9C), and impairs SOCE (Figure 8), with citations to Mo and Yang, 2018 and Yang et al., 2009.

claim: EHD2 deficiency reduced the cell surface levels of caveolae-associated ATP-sensitive K+ channels.
source: Consistent with this model, EHD2 deficiency reduced the cell surface levels of caveolae-associated ATP-sensitive K+ channels (Yang et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yang et al., 2018.

claim: Chemical inhibition of SOCE markedly impaired the pro-metastatic traits of EHD2-overexpressing TNBCs.
source: Finally, consistent with prior studies (Yang et al., 2009), chemical inhibition of SOCE markedly impaired the pro-metastatic traits of EHD2-overexpressing TNBCs, with a smaller impact on EHD2-KO cell lines (Figure 10A) and impaired the TNBC metastatic growth in vivo (Figure 10B).
evidence: SOCE inhibitors significantly reduced migration of wildtype TNBC cells (Figure 10A) and tumor growth in vivo (Figure 10B), with citation to Yang et al., 2009.

claim: SKF96365 targets additional Ca2+ channels besides Orai1.
source: However, since SKF96365 targets additional Ca2+ channels besides Orai1 (Ramsey et al., 2006; Ding et al., 2012), further studies using more selective inhibitors together with genetic analyses will be needed.
evidence: Supported by citations to Ramsey et al., 2006 and Ding et al., 2012.

claim: EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting.
source: Together, our studies support the idea that EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting, with EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression as predictors of response.
evidence: Based on findings that EHD2 regulates SOCE (Figure 8-9), SOCE inhibitors impair TNBC cell migration and tumor growth (Figure 10), and EHD2/CAV1/2 co-overexpression predicts poor survival (Figure 7B).

claim: EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression may serve as predictors of response to SOCE targeting.
source: Together, our studies support the idea that EHD2-overexpressing subsets of TNBC and other BC subtypes may be selectively amenable to SOCE targeting, with EHD2 and CAV1/2 overexpression as predictors of response.
evidence: Based on co-expression of EHD2 and CAV1/2 (Figure 7A), their association with poor survival (Figure 7B), and role in SOCE (Figure 8).
